question: What is preregistration and why is it important?
answer:
Preregistration is important for replications because it increases transparency and helps address skepticism [1]. Specifically, the specification of success criteria – a clear, advance statement of what results would count as a replication success or failure – is a key part of a preregistration [1]. A preregistration should also include an analysis plan, ideally with tested code, to safeguard against p-hacking [1]. 

Researchers are encouraged to adhere to the highest standards of openness and transparency, and can utilize preregistration templates found at [https://osf.io/7xrn9](https://osf.io/7xrn9) and [https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home](https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home) [1]. Replications can also be published as Registered Reports, where the methods are peer-reviewed *before* data collection, reducing bias [1]. A list of journals offering Registered Reports is [available online](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0) [1]. A special review platform for Registered Reports is Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI-RR; [https://rr.peercommunityin.org](https://rr.peercommunityin.org)) [1].

question: How is preregistration different from registered report?
answer:
Preregistration involves a clear, advance statement of success criteria and an analysis plan, ideally with tested code, to safeguard against p-hacking [1]. A preregistration without an analysis plan doesn’t offer this safeguard [1].

Registered Reports involve peer review and acceptance of methods *before* data collection [1]. This format is valuable for replications because acceptance isn’t based on the results, reducing bias towards smaller or null findings [1]. A list of journals offering Registered Reports is [available online](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0) [1]. Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI-RR) is a special review platform for Registered Reports: [https://rr.peercommunityin.org](https://rr.peercommunityin.org) [1].

question: What is open access and what are advantages and disadvantages?
answer:
According to the Transform to Open Science guide, open science is defined by the United States government as “the principle and practice of making research products and processes available to all, while respecting diverse cultures, maintaining security and privacy, and fostering collaborations, reproducibility, and equity” [1]. 

The guide states that open science increases access to knowledge and expands opportunities for participation [1]. It also leads to more transparent, replicable, and reproducible results [1]. The movement towards open science grew from advocating for inclusive labs and organizations, and from frustrations with accessing data, code, research methods, and publications [1].

The guide does not mention disadvantages of open access.

You can find more information at [https://forrt.org/transform-to-open-science-book/](https://forrt.org/transform-to-open-science-book/).

question: How can I make sure nobody misuses my openly available data?
answer:
The Open Research Toolkit encourages assigning the least restrictive Creative Commons License (CC-By) to all original materials, allowing anyone to use and adapt the work with attribution to the author [1]. 

Regarding misuse of openly available data, it is recommended to “Make all the materials associated with a research paper or book available online…Even if you do not share data, you can build an open workflow from the beginning that allows others to understand every step of the data generating process” [3].  You can also outline uncertainty in a pre-registration, stating when flexibility is and is not admissible [3].

question: How does open science reshape the future of interdisciplinary and collaborative research?
answer:
Open science promotes collaboration across fields and disciplines [1]. It encourages participation in scholarly events outside of psychology, such as the [Minority Politics Online Seminar Series](https://minoritypolitics.netlify.app/) [1]. Inviting speakers from other disciplines to department- or University-led symposiums, and initiating cross-discipline collaborations are also recommended [1]. 

The Many Babies project exemplifies this, using an open approach to research and collaborating with labs worldwide to replicate findings [2]. This project made all key decisions, data collection, and analysis openly accessible on GitHub ([https://github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public](https://github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public)) and the Open Science Framework ([https://osf.io/re95x/](https://osf.io/re95x/)) [2]. 

Furthermore, open science emphasizes shifting from competition to collaboration, encouraging scientists to work across departments or in multiple working groups [1]. The initiative “Open Science in the Developing World” highlights how community-led models are critical for capacity building and local ownership in collaborative research [4]. question: Can you generate detailed methodological steps based on queries to assist in experimental replication?
answer:
This handbook provides guidance on conducting reproductions and replications. Here's a breakdown of methodological steps based on the provided excerpts:

**1. Planning & Type Selection:**

*   Clarify whether the goal is to verify a method or test a broader theory, as this determines whether to pursue a close or conceptual approach [1].
*   Decide between reproduction and replication types using [Table 4.1](https://forrt.org/replication-handbook/planning.html#tbl-rep-types) to understand the different options and their goals [1].
*   Ideally, attempt a reproduction *before* conducting a replication to identify potential errors or inconsistencies [1].

**2. Execution:**

*   Gather all relevant materials from the original study [4].
*   If possible, numerically reproduce the original results using the original code and data [1]. Be aware of potential differences due to software versions or random number generators [1].
*   If code isn’t available, recreate analyses from the report, paying attention to data processing steps and handling of missing data [1].
*   Test the robustness of the original finding by making small alterations to the data processing and analyses [1].
*   Adhere to high standards of transparency, including detailed preregistration of hypotheses, analysis plans, and success criteria, ideally through Registered Reports [2].
*   If deviations from the preregistered plan occur, document and justify them transparently [2].
*   Consider using the small telescopes approach to determine the necessary sample size, focusing on whether the original study could detect the claimed effect [2].

**3. Analysis & Reporting:**

*   Run both the original statistical tests *and* more appropriate contemporary methods, if applicable [2].
*   Use balanced language when describing outcomes [4].
*   Carefully evaluate outcomes and potential reasons for divergences [4].
*   Report your research comprehensively and make it openly accessible [4].

question: What are the best practices for managing a successful laboratory and effective team?
answer:
According to the excerpt, several innovative mentoring practices can elevate your mentoring game [1]. These include rotating group meeting activities such as standard journal article discussion, EDI discussions, “Slide Improv”, and “Fact or Fiction” [1]. 

Specifically, the author suggests:

*   Rotating what you do in group meetings: standard journal article discussion, EDI discussion, “Slide Improv”, and Fact or Fiction [1].
*   Having students choose EDI articles from diverse areas [1].
*   Using “Slide Improv” to help students practice presenting and build confidence [1].
*   Using “Fact or Fiction” to develop critical thinking skills [1].
*   Conducting an anonymous poll once a year to assess lab quality of life and identify issues [1]. *   Providing new students with a document outlining expectations, tailored to their student level (Honours Thesis, MSc, or Ph.D.) [1].
*   Requiring students to list papers they’ve read with annotations explaining potential thesis citations every 6 months [1].

question: Was ist Präregistrierung und warum ist sie wichtig?
answer:
Präregistrierung ist besonders wichtig bei Replikationsstudien, da Replikationen oft mit Skepsis betrachtet werden [1]. Der Teil einer Präregistrierung, der am meisten bewirkt, ist die Spezifikation von Erfolgskriterien: eine klare, vorausschauende Aussage darüber, welche Ergebnisse als Replikationserfolg und welche als Misserfolg gelten würden [1]. Dies sollte mit einem Analyseplan (idealerweise mit Analysecode, der zuvor mit Testdaten oder Simulationen getestet wurde) kombiniert werden, da eine Präregistrierung ohne Analyseplan keinen Schutz vor P-Hacking bietet [1].

Es gibt eine spezielle Vorlage für die Präregistrierung von Brandt et al. ([2014](https://forrt.org/replication-handbook/references.html#ref-BrandtEtAl2014)), die jedoch möglicherweise nicht für die Struktur einiger Studien außerhalb der Sozialpsychologie geeignet ist (z. B. Persönlichkeitspsychologie oder kognitive Psychologie; eine Liste von Präregistrierungsvorlagen finden Sie unter [https://osf.io/7xrn9](https://osf.io/7xrn9) und [https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home](https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home)) [1].

Replikationen können auch als Registered Reports veröffentlicht werden, bei denen die Methoden vor der Datenerhebung begutachtet und zur Veröffentlichung akzeptiert werden [1]. Eine Liste von Fachzeitschriften, die Registered Reports anbieten (nicht speziell für Replikationen), ist [online verfügbar](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0) [1]. Eine spezielle Review-Plattform für Registered Reports ist Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI-RR; [https://rr.peercommunityin.org](https://rr.peercommunityin.org)) [1].

Feedback zum Handbuch ist willkommen an [lukas.roeseler@uni-muenster.de](mailto:lukas.roeseler@uni-muenster.de) oder [GitHub](https://github.com/forrtproject/replication-handbook/issues) [1].

question: ¿En qué se diferencia el prerregistro de un informe registrado?
answer:
La diferencia entre un preregistro y un informe registrado (Registered Report) radica en que en el informe registrado, los métodos son revisados por pares y aceptados para su publicación antes de la recolección de datos [1]. Esto reduce el sesgo a favor o en contra de los hallazgos nulos o inconclusivos que a menudo producen las replicaciones, ya que la decisión de aceptación ya no depende de los resultados [1].

Para más información sobre preregistros, puede consultar esta plantilla [<https://osf.io/7xrn9>] [1] o esta wiki [<https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home>] [1]. También puede encontrar una lista de revistas que ofrecen Registered Reports aquí [<https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0>] [1]. Existe una plataforma de revisión específica para Registered Reports llamada Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI-RR) [<https://rr.peercommunityin.org>] [1].

question: Ön kayıt nedir ve neden önemlidir?
answer:
Ön kayıt, bir replikasyon çalışmasının başarısı için kritik öneme sahiptir. Çünkü replikasyonların genellikle şüpheyle karşılandığı durumlarda, araştırmacıların en yüksek düzeyde açıklık ve şeffaflıkla hareket etmelerini teşvik eder [2]. Ön kaydın en önemli kısmı, başarı kriterlerinin açık ve önceden belirtilmesidir; yani hangi sonuçların bir replikasyonun başarısı, hangilerinin başarısızlık sayılacağını önceden tanımlamaktır [2]. Bu, analiz planıyla (tercihen test verileri veya simülasyonlarla test edilmiş analiz koduyla) birlikte yapılmalıdır, çünkü analiz planı olmayan bir ön kayıt, p-hacking'e karşı koruma sağlamaz [2].

Ön kayıt, araştırmacıların bir replikasyonu yakın veya kavramsal olarak yapmaya karar vermesine yardımcı olur [3]. Ayrıca, bir replikasyon çalışmasına başlamadan önce orijinal bulgunun yeniden üretilebilirliğini değerlendirmek önemlidir [3].

question: Akademide kariyer ilerlemesi için gereken temel beceriler nelerdir?
answer:
Akademik bir kariyerde ilerlemek için gereken temel beceriler hakkında metinlerde çeşitli bilgilere rastlanmaktadır.

*   Doktora derecesi sonrası iş başvurularında transkriptten ziyade yayınların sayısı ve kalitesi önemlidir [1]. Özellikle akademik pozisyonlar için yayınlar belirleyici rol oynar.
*   Araştırma tasarımı ve proje yönetimi becerileri önemlidir. Bir doktora derecesi, bu becerileri geliştirmenize yardımcı olur [1].
*   Veri analizi ve istatistiksel yöntemler bilgisi gereklidir. Özellikle inferansiyel istatistikler akademik araştırmalarda sıklıkla kullanılır [3]. Ancak, bazı durumlarda (örneğin, organizasyonel verilerle çalışırken) tanımlayıcı istatistikler de büyük önem taşır [3].
*   Sunum becerileri önemlidir. Hem yazılı (tezler, makaleler) hem de sözlü (konferanslar, seminerler) sunum yapabilmek gerekir [1].
*   İngilizce bilgisi gereklidir. Yayın yapmak ve uluslararası konferanslara katılmak için İngilizce bilmek önemlidir.
*   İşbirliği ve iletişim becerileri önemlidir. Diğer araştırmacılarla işbirliği yapmak ve fikir alışverişinde bulunmak akademik kariyerin önemli bir parçasıdır [2].
*   Eleştirel düşünme becerisi önemlidir. Bir araştırmanın güçlü ve zayıf yönlerini değerlendirebilmek ve yeni fikirler üretebilmek gerekir [2].
*   Uyarlanabilirlik ve öğrenmeye açıklık önemlidir. Akademik dünya sürekli değişiyor ve yeni teknolojiler ve yöntemler ortaya çıkıyor. Bu değişikliklere ayak uydurabilmek ve sürekli öğrenmek gerekir [3].

Ek olarak, [2] adresinde bulunan makalede, anonim anketler aracılığıyla öğrencilerin geri bildirimlerini almak ve mentorluk becerilerini geliştirmek için yenilikçi yöntemler önerilmektedir. Bu da akademik kariyerde başarılı olmak için önemli bir beceri olan öğrenci odaklılığı ve sürekli gelişime açıklığı vurgulamaktadır.

question: Che cos'è la preregistrazione e perché è importante?
answer:
La preregistrazione è incoraggiata per le replicazioni, in quanto specifica i criteri di successo: una dichiarazione chiara e preventiva di quali risultati costituirebbero un successo o un fallimento della replicazione [1]. Questo, abbinato a un piano di analisi (idealmente con codice di analisi testato in precedenza), protegge dal p-hacking [1].

È importante perché, dato che le replicazioni sono spesso accolte con scetticismo, aderire agli standard più elevati di apertura e trasparenza è fondamentale [1]. Esistono modelli di preregistrazione, come quello di Brandt et al. ([2014](https://forrt.org/replication-handbook/references.html#ref-BrandtEtAl2014)), e si possono trovare altri modelli qui: [https://osf.io/7xrn9](https://osf.io/7xrn9) e [https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home](https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home) [1].

Le replicazioni possono anche essere pubblicate come Registered Reports, dove i metodi sono sottoposti a revisione paritaria e accettati per la pubblicazione prima della raccolta dei dati [1]. Una lista di riviste che offrono Registered Reports è [disponibile online](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0) [1]. Esiste anche una piattaforma di revisione specifica per Registered Reports, Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI-RR; [https://rr.peercommunityin.org](https://rr.peercommunityin.org)) [1].

question: पूर्व-पंजीकरण (प्रीरजिस्ट्रेशन) क्या है और यह क्यों महत्वपूर्ण है?
answer:
पूर्व-पंजीकरण (प्रीरजिस्ट्रेशन) एक स्पष्ट, अग्रिम कथन है कि कौन से परिणाम प्रतिकृति सफलता माने जाएंगे और कौन से विफलता [1]। यह महत्वपूर्ण है क्योंकि प्रतिकृतियों को अक्सर संदेह के साथ देखा जाता है, इसलिए उच्चतम स्तर की पारदर्शिता और खुलेपन का पालन करना प्रोत्साहित किया जाता है [1]। पूर्व-पंजीकरण पी-हैकिंग से सुरक्षा प्रदान करता है, खासकर जब विश्लेषण योजना के साथ जोड़ा जाता है [1]।

इसके अतिरिक्त, प्रतिकृति अध्ययनों के लिए, पूर्व-पंजीकरण का सबसे महत्वपूर्ण हिस्सा सफलता मानदंड का निर्धारण है [1]। Boyce et al. ([2024](https://forrt.org/replication-handbook/references.html#ref-BoyceEtAl2024)) ने यह भी पाया कि स्पष्ट कमजोरियों को ठीक किए बिना असफल प्रतिकृतियों को दोहराने से परिणाम नहीं बदले [1]।

आप Brandt et al. ([2014](https://forrt.org/replication-handbook/references.html#ref-BrandtEtAl2014)) द्वारा एक विशिष्ट पूर्व-पंजीकरण टेम्पलेट पा सकते हैं, हालांकि यह सभी अध्ययनों के लिए उपयुक्त नहीं हो सकता है [1]। अन्य टेम्पलेट यहां उपलब्ध हैं: [https://osf.io/7xrn9](https://osf.io/7xrn9) और [https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home](https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home) [1]।

Registered Reports के रूप में प्रतिकृतियों को प्रकाशित करना भी संभव है, जहां डेटा एकत्र करने से पहले विधियों की सहकर्मी समीक्षा की जाती है और प्रकाशन के लिए स्वीकार किया जाता है [1]। Registered Reports की पेशकश करने वाले जर्नलों की एक सूची यहां उपलब्ध है: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0) [1]।

Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI-RR) एक विशेष समीक्षा मंच है: [https://rr.peercommunityin.org](https://rr.peercommunityin.org) [1]।

question: शिक्षा जगत में करियर में आगे बढ़ने के लिए कौन-से मुख्य कौशल आवश्यक हैं?
answer:
शिक्षा जगत में करियर में आगे बढ़ने के लिए आवश्यक मुख्य कौशल के बारे में जानकारी सीधे तौर पर दिए गए अंशों में नहीं है। हालांकि, अंश [1] में बताया गया है कि डेटा और अनुसंधान कौशल गैर-शैक्षणिक नौकरी में महत्वपूर्ण हैं। इसमें डेटा को जोड़ना, डेटाबेस का उपयोग करना (जैसे SQL), और सांख्यिकीय सोच शामिल है। यह भी उल्लेख किया गया है कि शैक्षणिक डेटा की तुलना में वास्तविक दुनिया का डेटा अधिक जटिल होता है [1]।

question: पूर्वनोंदणी (प्रीरजिस्ट्रेशन) म्हणजे काय आणि ती का महत्त्वाची आहे?
answer:
पूर्वनोंदणी (प्रीरजिस्ट्रेशन) म्हणजे अभ्यासाची योजना, गृहितके, विश्लेषण योजना आणि यश निकष (success criteria) अभ्यास सुरू करण्यापूर्वीच स्पष्टपणे नोंदवणे. हे संशोधनात पारदर्शकता आणि कठोरता आणण्यासाठी महत्त्वाचे आहे. विशेषत: प्रतिकृती अभ्यासांमध्ये (replication studies) हे खूप उपयुक्त ठरते, कारण यामुळे निकालांमध्ये पूर्वग्रह (publication bias) टाळता येतो [1].

प्रतिकृती अभ्यासांमध्ये, पूर्वनोंदणीचा सर्वात महत्त्वाचा भाग म्हणजे यशाचे निकष निश्चित करणे - कोणते निकाल अभ्यासाची पुनरावृत्ती यशस्वी ठरवतील आणि कोणते अयशस्वी, हे स्पष्टपणे नमूद करणे [1]. यासोबतच, विश्लेषणाची योजना (analysis plan) आणि शक्य असल्यास, विश्लेषण कोड (analysis code) देखील नमूद करावा. कारण, पूर्वनोंदणीशिवाय विश्लेषण योजना नसेल, तर 'पी-हॅकिंग' (p-hacking) टाळता येणार नाही [1].

तुम्ही खालील ठिकाणी पूर्वनोंदणी टेम्पलेट (preregistration template) शोधू शकता:
* [https://osf.io/7xrn9](https://osf.io/7xrn9)
* [https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home](https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home)

तसेच, Registered Reports च्या माध्यमातून प्रतिकृती अभ्यास प्रकाशित करणे अधिक फायदेशीर आहे, कारण या स्वरूपात पद्धतींचे पुनरावलोकन (peer-review) डेटा गोळा करण्यापूर्वीच केले जाते. त्यामुळे, लहान, शून्य किंवा अनिर्णायक निष्कर्षांमधील पूर्वग्रहांना (bias) कमी करता येते [1]. Registered Reports देणाऱ्या जर्नल्सची यादी येथे उपलब्ध आहे: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0).

question: शैक्षणिक क्षेत्रात कारकिर्दीत प्रगती करण्यासाठी कोणती मुख्य कौशल्ये आवश्यक आहेत?
answer:
शैक्षणिक क्षेत्रात कारकिर्दीत प्रगती करण्यासाठी आवश्यक असलेल्या मुख्य कौशल्यांविषयी माहिती खालीलप्रमाणे आहे:

FORRT च्या दृष्टिकोनातून, 'सिद्धांत आधारित शिक्षण' (Principled Education) महत्त्वाचे आहे. यात खुले आणि पुनरुत्पादक विज्ञान (open and reproducible science) पद्धतींचा वापर करणे, विज्ञानाला ज्ञानाचा संग्रह न मानता एक प्रक्रिया म्हणून शिकवणे, तसेच शिकवण्याची सामग्री सार्वजनिकरित्या सामायिक करणे इत्यादींचा समावेश होतो [1].

यासाठी काही उपयुक्त सूचना:

*   तुमच्या सध्याच्या शिकवण्याच्या पद्धतींचे मूल्यांकन करा आणि त्या खुल्या विज्ञानाच्या तत्त्वांवर आधारित आहेत का ते तपासा [1].
*   अभ्यासक्रमात खुल्या विज्ञानाशी संबंधित साहित्य आणि असाइनमेंट समाविष्ट करा [1].
*   शिकवण्यासाठी लागणारी सामग्री तयार करा, पुन्हा वापरा आणि इतरांना सामायिक करा [1].
*   विद्यार्थ्यांना खुल्या विज्ञानाच्या प्रकल्पांमध्ये सहभागी होण्याची संधी द्या [1].
*   विविधता, समानता आणि समावेश (Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion - DEI) या विषयांना तुमच्या शिकवणीत आणि मार्गदर्शन पद्धतीत समाविष्ट करा [1].
*   शैक्षणिक संस्थेत 'सिद्धांत आधारित शिक्षणा'चा पुरस्कार करा [1].

याव्यतिरिक्त, गुणात्मक संशोधनामध्ये (Qualitative research) सांस्कृतिक नम्रता (cultural humility) आणि विविधतेचा आदर करणे महत्त्वाचे आहे [2]. संशोधकांनी त्यांच्या कार्यामध्ये पारदर्शकता (transparency) राखणे, डेटा आणि सामग्री सामायिक करणे, तसेच नैतिक विचार करणे आवश्यक आहे [2].

question: ಪೂರ್ವನೋಂದಣಿ (ಪ್ರಿರಿಜಿಸ್ಟ್ರೇಷನ್) ಎಂದರೇನು ಮತ್ತು ಅದು ಏಕೆ ಮುಖ್ಯ?
answer:
ಪ್ರೂರ್ವನೋಂದಣಿ (ಪ್ರಿರಿಜಿಸ್ಟ್ರೇಷನ್) ಎಂದರೆ ಫಲಿತಾಂಶಗಳನ್ನು ನೋಡಿದ ನಂತರ ಬದಲಾಗದಂತೆ, ಅಧ್ಯಯನದ ಯೋಚನೆಗಳು, ವಿಶ್ಲೇಷಣೆ ಯೋಜನೆಗಳು ಮತ್ತು ಯಶಸ್ಸಿನ ಮಾನದಂಡಗಳನ್ನು ಮುಂಚಿತವಾಗಿ ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟವಾಗಿ ಬರೆಯುವುದು. ಇದು ಪ್ರಕಟಣೆ ಪಕ್ಷಪಾತವನ್ನು (ಪಬ್ಲಿಕೇಶನ್ ಬಯಾಸ್) ತಡೆಯಲು ಸಹಾಯ ಮಾಡುತ್ತದೆ [1].

ಪ್ರೂರ್ವನೋಂದಣಿಗಳು ಬಹಳ ಮುಖ್ಯ ಏಕೆಂದರೆ ಪುನರಾವೃತ್ತಿ ಅಧ್ಯయనಗಳು (ರೆಪ್ಲಿಕೇಶನ್ ಸ್ಟಡೀಸ್‌) ಹೆಚ್ಚಾಗಿ ಸಂದೇಹದಿಂದ ನೋಡಲ್ಪಡುತ್ತವೆ. ಇದು ಬಹಿರಂಗತೆ ಮತ್ತು ಪಾರದರ್ಶಕತೆಯನ್ನು ಹೆಚ್ಚಿಸುತ್ತದೆ [1]. ಪೂರ್ವನೋಂದಣೆಯು ವಿಶ್ಲೇಷಣೆ ಯೋಜನೆಯನ್ನು ಒಳಗೊಂಡಿರಬೇಕು, ಮತ್ತು ಸಾಧ್ಯವಾದರೆ, ಪರೀಕ್ಷಿಸಿದ ಕೋಡ್‌ನೊಂದಿಗೆ, ಏಕೆಂದರೆ ಪೂರ್ವನೋಂದಣಿ ಇಲ್ಲದೆ ವಿಶ್ಲೇಷಣೆ ಯೋಜನೆ, p-ಹ್ಯಾಕಿಂಗ್‌ನಿಂದ ರಕ್ಷಣೆ ನೀಡುವುದಿಲ್ಲ [1].

ನೀವು ಇಲ್ಲಿ ಪ್ರೂರ್ವನೋಂದಣಿ ಟೆಂಪ್ಲೇಟ್‌ಗಳನ್ನು ಕಾಣಬಹುದು: [https://osf.io/7xrn9](https://osf.io/7xrn9) ಮತ್ತು [https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home](https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home) [1].

ಹೆಚ್ಚಿನ ಮಾಹಿತಿಗಾಗಿ ಅಥವಾ ಪ್ರತಿಕ್ರಿಯೆಗಾಗಿ, ಇಲ್ಲಿ ಸಂಪರ್ಕಿಸಬಹುದು: [lukas.roeseler@uni-muenster.de](mailto:lukas.roeseler@uni-muenster.de) ಅಥವಾ [GitHub](https://github.com/forrtproject/replication-handbook/issues) [1][3].

question: What does transparency mean in research?
answer:
According to the United States government, open science – and therefore transparency in research – is “the principle and practice of making research products and processes available to all, while respecting diverse cultures, maintaining security and privacy, and fostering collaborations, reproducibility, and equity.” [1] This openness increases access to knowledge and expands opportunities for participation, leading to more transparent and replicable results. [1]

I cannot tell you whether your preregistration draft will be accepted, as acceptance depends on the review process of the specific journal or platform you submit to [1].

question: Can you write the results section of my paper based on my SPSS output?
answer:
Evaluating replication findings is complex, and describing them as simply “successful” or “failed” is an oversimplification [1]. Conclusions depend on statistical criteria, like effect size comparisons, and how differences between original and replication studies are interpreted [1]. Clear preregistration and transparency about theoretically central effects are essential [1].

When findings diverge, careful interpretation is required, as discrepancies may stem from limitations in validity—statistical, internal, construct, or external—in either the original or replication study [1]. Hidden moderators may also influence outcomes [1]. Replication results should be evaluated in terms of methodological closeness and interpreted within a broader theoretical framework to assess robustness and generalizability [1].  Original authors can be invited for comments, and some journals require such statements [1].

There is no strong consensus on what constitutes replication success, and some approaches can be biased or imprecise [1]. Researchers face a trade-off between categorizing results and making a clear decision about the outcome [1]. question: How to eliminate ghost authorship in scientific publishing?
answer:
The Academic Wheel of Privilege (AWoP) is a tool designed to guide equitable authorship order decisions [1]. It aims to reform authorship practices and inspire a broader transformation towards fairness and inclusiveness in the academic landscape [1]. The AWoP helps users actively identify and consider privilege in authorship decisions, facilitating equitable and transparent authorship order determination [1].

The AWoP toolkit includes resources such as a manuscript ([https://doi.org/10.31222/osf.io/af4nk_v2](https://doi.org/10.31222/osf.io/af4nk_v2)), a web app ([Access the AWoP Web App](https://forrt.org/awop_app/)), an OSF page with supplementary files ([https://osf.io/pfxqb/overview](https://osf.io/pfxqb/overview)), reflection questions, case studies, illustrated examples, a detailed bibliography, and a syllabus [1]. 

Reviewer Zero also advocates for collaboration and conversation to advance diversity, equity, and inclusion in peer review systems and open science [2]. They suggest that if you have experience in scientific publication, you should speak about your rejections as well as your successes and amplify the voices of people whose voices are not yet central to the conversation [2].

You can find more information about the AWoP and contact them at [awop@forrt.org](mailto:awop@forrt.org) [1]. You can also stay updated on Reviewer Zero’s activities at [www.reviewerzero.net](http://www.reviewerzero.net) and explore their on-demand resources [2].

answer:

question: Can I preregister a study that uses existing/secondary data?
answer:
Yes, you can preregister a study that uses existing/secondary data [2]. Preregistrations contain a description of the planned study or analysis prior to its execution, and can reduce researchers’ ‘degrees of freedom’ [1]. In the case of reproductions, preregistering the analysis plan ensures clarity and prevents unintended flexibility in how the data are analyzed [1]. While a numerical reproduction with available code does not *require* preregistration, it is recommended to a priori specify all further planned analyses [1]. Even if the data could already have been accessed, starting with preregistration is still recommended as a commitment device [2]. 

You can find more information about preregistration in Section 5.4 of the handbook [1].

question: What is FORRT and Open Science?
answer:
FORRT brings the open scholarship and reproducible science movements to teaching and mentoring, aiming to build a pathway for educators to adopt these tenets [1]. Its mission is to achieve the best conceivable practices in higher education [1].

FORRT’s goals include creating a space for educators to support each other, supporting scholars in staying up-to-date on best practices, advocating for greater institutional recognition of teaching and mentoring, facilitating conversations about the ethics of science, and fostering social justice through democratization of scientific resources [1]. 

Open Science is a key area of focus, with a project called POSTEdu – Promoting Open Science Teaching – designed to equip the next generation of researchers and consumers of science with the knowledge of open and reproducible research [2]. This project, funded by the Dutch Research Council (NWO), aims to develop a self-guided program with three modules for educators interested in teaching Open Science through a positive, participatory, and inclusive lens [2]. The modules will cover topics like the ethos of Open Science, student-led research, and incorporating diversity and inclusion [2].

You can find more information about FORRT’s clusters here: [https://forrt.org/clusters/](https://forrt.org/clusters/) and about the POSTEdu project here: [https://forrt.org/teaching_os/](https://forrt.org/teaching_os/).

question: Since preregistration forbids exploratory analyses, how should I report unexpected findings?
answer:
According to the handbook, researchers should adhere to the highest standards of openness and transparency when executing replications, including detailed preregistration of hypotheses, analysis plans, and success criteria [2]. A preregistration without an analysis plan provides no safeguard against p-hacking [2]. 

However, analyses of replication results are often a compromise or a combination of the original analysis and the current state-of-the-art [2]. Researchers should follow the original analysis plan as closely as possible, but also examine their raw data to check for distributional anomalies and report relevant sensitivity checks [2]. If methodological advances suggest the original statistical tests are not robust, researchers may want to run both the original test and the most appropriate statistical approach [2].

question: Since the Open Science Collaboration (2015) showed 90% of psychology studies failed to replicate, should I distrust all psychology?
answer:
“A Student’s Guide to Open Science” was written to address the lack of discussion around replication issues in psychology teaching [1]. The author, Charlotte Pennington, felt like a failure when she couldn’t replicate classic effects during her PhD in 2016, and realized these experiences were common but not discussed in the literature [1]. 

The book aims to provide a resource for students and educators to understand the replication crisis, its causes (like academic incentive structures and cognitive biases), and open science reform [1]. It includes a guide to implementing open science practices such as preprints, preregistration, Registered Reports, and open materials, data, and code [1]. Pedagogic resources are included, such as activities where students can plan a replication and preregister it using templates from repositories like AsPredicted.org/Open Science Framework [1].

You can find additional resources from FORRT, including a [bank of lesson plans](https://forrt.org/lesson-plans), [replications and reversals](https://forrt.org/reversals), and [open science glossary](https://forrt.org/glossary) [1]. Other key resources mentioned include [RIOT Science Club](https://web.archive.org/web/20260317091517/https://www.riotscience.co.uk/), [ReproducibiliTea Journal Clubs](https://reproducibilitea.org/), the podcast [Everything Hertz](https://web.archive.org/web/20260122061515/https://everythinghertz.com/), the [UKRN](https://www.ukrn.org/) and their [primers on open science practices](https://www.ukrn.org/primers/), the [Open Research Calendar](https://openresearchcalendar.org/), and [MetaArXiv](https://osf.io/preprints/metaarxiv/) [1].

question: How should I supervise a master's thesis that is designed as a replication study?
answer:
Here's what the handbook excerpts say about conducting and supervising replication studies:

Reproductions should ideally take place before replication studies to investigate the correctness of the original report [1]. This helps uncover coding errors, fraud, robustness to analytical decisions, and generalizability [1]. 

When planning a replication, it's important to decide whether to conduct a close or conceptual replication, depending on whether the focus is on a method or a theory [1]. Table 4.1 provides an overview of different types of repetitive research [1]: [<https://forrt.org/replication-handbook/planning.html#tbl-rep-types>].

High standards of transparency are essential, including detailed preregistration of hypotheses, analysis plans, and success criteria, ideally through Registered Reports [2]. Sample size justification should go beyond simply matching the original study, and deviations from the original study should be transparently documented and justified [2]. 

Piloting can identify procedural flaws, and collaborating with the original authors can be helpful [2]. 

A checklist summarizing core recommendations for planning, conducting, and reporting reproductions and replications is available [4]: [<https://forrt.org/replication-handbook/appendix_checklist.html>].

You can provide feedback on this handbook to [lukas.roeseler@uni-muenster.de](mailto:lukas.roeseler@uni-muenster.de) or via [GitHub](https://github.com/forrtproject/replication-handbook/issues) [1][3][4].

question: Does FORRT have a glossary of open science terms? Also, what is the difference between a preregistration and a registered report?
answer:
Yes, FORRT has a glossary of open science terms [1]. The glossary aims to clarify terminology related to open scholarship and reduce barriers to entry for those unfamiliar with the field [1]. It originated from a crowd-sourced project involving over 110 collaborators who defined and reviewed upwards of 250 terms [1]. Phase 2 of the glossary project is currently open, inviting contributions to improve existing definitions, extend the scope of terms, and translate them into other languages [1]. You can find the glossary [here](https://forrt.org/glossary/english/).

Regarding the difference between a preregistration and a registered report: a preregistration involves a clear, advance statement of success criteria and an analysis plan to prevent publication bias [2]. A Registered Report takes this a step further – the methods are peer-reviewed and accepted for publication *before* data are collected [2]. This reduces bias towards smaller or null findings often produced by replications [2]. You can find a list of journals offering Registered Reports [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0) and a special review platform for Registered Reports [here](https://rr.peercommunityin.org) [2].

question: How can I make my analysis code reproducible for others?
answer:
To make your analysis reproducible, you should report software details transparently, including the version of the software and any additional packages or plug-ins used [1]. For R users, the `sessionInfo` function provides a comprehensive overview, and for Python users, the `session_info.show` package can be used [1]. You can find the Python package at [https://gitlab.com/joelostblom/session_info](https://gitlab.com/joelostblom/session_info) [1].

Additionally, reproduction studies should clearly report resource availability, such as raw data, cleaning code, and analysis code [1]. 

If you have feedback on this preliminary version of the handbook, you can contact [lukas.roeseler@uni-muenster.de](mailto:lukas.roeseler@uni-muenster.de) or submit issues on [GitHub](https://github.com/forrtproject/replication-handbook/issues) [1][2].

question: How can I share interview transcripts openly while protecting my participants?
answer:
Researchers can share interview protocols, memos, coding notebooks, tools (such as Nvivo or R packages), or even the data itself, but must consider ethical boundaries [1]. Specifically, researchers must include their plan within their consent procedures and IRB protocols to not violate any ethical boundaries when sharing materials [1]. The extent of what is shared exists on a spectrum, and access can be limited to specific groups like dissertation committees, participants, or reviewers [1].

For feedback or to contribute to the conversation, you can contact Rachel Renbarger at rachelrenbarger (at) gmail.com [1].

You can also find more information and resources on the [FORRT website](https://forrt.org/) [2].

question: Which tools can check the statistics reported in a paper for errors?
answer:
ReproCrowd is a crowdsourced platform for numerical reproductions that uses an AI-assisted workflow to rebuild a paper's analysis and check whether the numbers reproduce [1]. It allows users to run a reproducibility check using an app [1]. 

Here are the steps to use ReproCrowd:

*   Choose an article with openly available data and copy its DOI [1].
*   Run the reproducibility check using the [ReproCrowd app](https://forrt.org/reprocrowd/) [1].
*   Check and sign the result with your name and ORCID [1].
*   Share and compare the results, which are deposited on Zenodo [1].

You can [Download the latest release](https://github.com/forrtproject/reprocrowd-app/releases) of the ReproCrowd app or [View source on GitHub](https://github.com/forrtproject/reprocrowd-app) [1].

question: What is analytic flexibility and why can it be problematic in research?
answer:
Analytic flexibility, referred to as “researcher degrees of freedom”, refers to the numerous methodological choices available in neuroimaging research, particularly with high-dimensional MRI data [1]. This includes choices about where to look for effects in the brain and how to define significance given a large number of tests [1]. 

This flexibility can be problematic because it can lead to variability in results, even when analyzing the same dataset [1]. A study observed that 70 independent analysis teams, using the same fMRI dataset and predefined hypotheses, produced substantially different results due to variations in their analysis pipelines . This highlights how many options exist, such as defining regions of interest anatomically or functionally, and choosing different methods for multiple testing corrections . The high number of researcher degrees of freedom, combined with low statistical power and potential bias, can drive false-positive findings [1].

You can find more information on references cited in the text here: <https://forrt.org/replication-handbook/references.html> 
You can also find a template for preregistrations specific to fMRI studies here: <https://doi.org/10.23668/psycharchives.5121> .

question: What does Critiquing After the Results are Known (CARKing) mean in research?
answer:
I could not find information about "CARKing" in the provided excerpts. However, the excerpts discuss reproductions and replications in detail. 

Reproductions and replications are gaining traction in the social sciences due to failures to reproduce and replicate published findings [2]. A reproduction involves retesting previously examined hypotheses, while replication uses new data [3]. Reproductions often serve as a cost-efficient first step to verify the reliability of results before attempting a replication [3].

The closeness between the original and repeated study can influence outcomes, with even minor differences potentially affecting results [1][3]. Numerical and robustness reproductions help confirm findings, while conceptual replications test generalizability [3]. 

Researchers should ideally investigate a finding’s reproducibility and robustness *before* conducting a replication study [1]. If the original code and data are available, researchers can attempt to numerically reproduce the results, but differences in software or settings may require corrections [1]. If no analysis script is available, analyses need to be recreated from the report [1].

question: What is computational reproducibility in research, and why is it important?
answer:
Computational reproducibility refers to the ability to re-run an analysis and obtain the same results, and is a key aspect of reproducibility in research [4]. It’s important because it allows independent researchers to verify findings and assess research quality [4]. 

The iRISE consortium and FORRT collaborated on a scoping review to identify reproducibility metrics, finding 50 metrics used to quantify reproducibility, with 74% being statistical formulas or models [4]. They found that many replication projects don’t clearly define how they measure reproducibility, and the choice of metric should depend on the study’s goals [4]. 

You can find an extended and interactive table summarizing these metrics at [http://rachelhey.github.io/reproducibility_metrics/](http://rachelhey.github.io/reproducibility_metrics/) [4].

question: What is a conceptual replication in research, and why is it important?
answer:
A conceptual replication involves conducting a study with changes that may be theoretically relevant, but still tests the same hypothesis – for example, using a different operationalization [4]. It aims to test the generalizability of the original finding and the validity of the theory [1][4]. 

It is important because, while close replications test the credibility of original results, conceptual replications are concerned with generalizability [4]. They help determine if a finding holds true under different conditions or with different methods [4]. Furthermore, conceptual replications can help specify the boundaries of a claim, especially when the original authors did not clearly define the scope of their findings [4]. 

According to Schöch , replications – including conceptual replications – use a similar method to a previous study but with different data [4].

question: What are Constraints on Generality (COG) and why are they important in research reporting?
answer:
The excerpts discuss the generalizability crisis in research [1][2]. This crisis arises from factors limiting the extent to which research findings can be applied to broader populations [1]. Several case studies illustrate this, including studies with limited demographic representation in samples [1]. 

Specifically, the excerpts highlight that some studies have found treatments may be less effective for Black patients due to differences in skin biology [1], that clinical trials often underrepresent racial and ethnic minorities [1], and that studies have historically focused on men, leading to inaccurate treatment recommendations for women [1]. Additionally, genetic research has been criticized for focusing on populations of European ancestry [1], and mental health studies may not be applicable to non-Western cultures [1].

To address these issues, researchers are encouraged to report sample demographics [2], acknowledge their positionality [2], and consider context and identity in their research [2]. The excerpts also recommend using open science practices, such as preregistering studies and sharing data [2][3]. 

Regarding publishing replication research, the excerpts note that some journals reject replications due to a lack of novelty [3]. However, several journals dedicated to replications are listed, including: [Journal of Comments and Replications in Economics](https://jcr-econ.org), [Replication Research](https://replicationresearch.org), [Journal of Open Psychology Data](https://openpsychologydata.metajnl.com), [Journal of Robustness Reports](https://scipost.org/JRobustRep), [Rescience C](https://rescience.github.io), [Journal of Management Scientific Reports](https://smgmt.org/jomsr), [Rescience X](http://rescience.org/x), and [Implementation and Replication Studies in Mathematics Education](https://brill.com/view/journals/irme/irme-overview.xml) [3].

question: What are equivalence tests and how do they work in assessing meaningful effects in research?
answer:
Equivalence testing determines if the replication study finds an effect that is equally negligible, when testing for original null findings [2]. It falls under approaches to assessing replication success and is categorized as “Different data - same analysis” [2]. 

Specifically, equivalence testing asks whether the results from the replication study are statistically equivalent to the results of the original study [2].

Open science increases access to knowledge and expands opportunities for participation, leading to more transparent, replicable, and reproducible results [1]. It requires changing how we work to move forward together [1].

Principled teaching exposes students to a more honest educational process and trains them to be good consumers of science [3]. Principled mentoring enables students to see their work contribute meaningfully to the scientific community and fosters curiosity and problem-solving [3].

question: What are open materials in research, and why are they important for reproducibility?
answer:
The Open Research Toolkit provides resources for learning about and implementing open research principles [1]. It was created by Christopher Eaker, who began developing it after recognizing the need to situate his data curation work within the broader context of open research [1]. The toolkit aims to help librarians and others skill up on open research practices [1].

The modules in the Open Research Toolkit cover topics such as the open research ecosystem, open access, FAIR data principles, and open peer review [1]. Each module includes a slide deck, presentation notes, a narrated video, and a bibliography [1]. These materials are available on the [Open Science Framework](https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/A4FTW) and YouTube ([http://doi.org/10.7290/ORT_Videos](http://doi.org/10.7290/ORT_Videos)) [1]. 

According to the “Positive Changes from the Replication Crisis” page, open science involves making research products and processes available to all, increasing access to knowledge and opportunities for participation [2].  It’s important because sharing data, code, results, and knowledge leads to more transparent, replicable, and reproducible results [2].  Specifically, procedural changes now include tools for statistical assessment and multiverse analysis to ensure the robustness of findings [2].  Community changes include the formation of open science communities like ReproducibiliTea and FORRT [2].

The TOPS Open Science 101 guide defines open science as making research products and processes available to all, fostering collaborations, reproducibility, and equity [3]. It emphasizes that open science aims for inclusivity and accessibility in research [3].

question: What is the PRO (peer review openness) initiative and what conditions does it require for peer reviewing a manuscript?
answer:
Reviewer Zero is a collective founded in 2020 to improve the culture of scientific peer review [1]. They collaborate with FORRT to develop a train-the-trainer program [2]. 

Open peer review, which includes disclosure of author and reviewer identities and reviews, is one innovation in the peer review process [1]. However, individuals who occupy less powerful positions may experience backlash or have their perspectives dismissed in identified peer review [1]. Transparent peer review, where reviews are public but reviewer identities are not, might offer greater security to reviewers [1]. 

The newsletter highlights that inequities in peer review need to be addressed before open review can serve a wide range of scholars [2]. It also mentions that hostile or unprofessional reviews can be common, and individuals from historically excluded groups might avoid participating in open review processes [1].

You can find more information about Reviewer Zero at [http://www.reviewerzero.net](http://www.reviewerzero.net) [1] and on [Twitter](https://twitter.com/reviewer_zero) [2]. You can also join the FORRT Slack channel to get involved [https://join.slack.com/t/forrt/shared_invite/zt-alobr3z7-NOR0mTBfD1vKXn9qlOKqaQ](https://join.slack.com/t/forrt/shared_invite/zt-alobr3z7-NOR0mTBfD1vKXn9qlOKqaQ) [2].

question: What does statistical significance mean in the context of Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST)?
answer:
Evaluating replication findings is complex, and describing results as simply “successful” or “failed” is an oversimplification [1]. Conclusions depend on statistical criteria, like effect size comparisons, and how differences between original and replication studies are interpreted [1]. 

Like in classical Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST), replication researchers face a trade-off between categorizing outcomes (success vs. failure) and making a clear decision [1]. Replication researchers need to specify which effects are of primary interest in their preregistration and how they will aggregate results [1].

You can find more information about references related to this topic here: [https://forrt.org/replication-handbook/references.html#ref-SchauerHedges2021](https://forrt.org/replication-handbook/references.html#ref-SchauerHedges2021) and [https://forrt.org/replication-handbook/references.html#ref-PatilEtAl2016b](https://forrt.org/replication-handbook/references.html#ref-PatilEtAl2016b).

You can also find Julia Strand's course materials on Psychology’s Credibility Revolution here: [https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/e/2PACX-1vREwmeADm5WZCBfjAKyAkzYC_cQb7xtYv6C7e_wBJx0BUhJ3lFY0WABpIb0XotJake0Xrh-CC6g1Vwy/pub?start=false&loop=false&delayms=99999999&slide=id.g93d3e0908d_0_316](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/e/2PACX-1vREwmeADm5WZCBfjAKyAkzYC_cQb7xtYv6C7e_wBJx0BUhJ3lFY0WABpIb0XotJake0Xrh-CC6g1Vwy/pub?start=false&loop=false&delayms=99999999&slide=id.g93d3e0908d_0_316).

question: What is a transparency checklist and how does it support researchers and reviewers in scientific research?
answer:
A Transparency Checklist is an educational tool used to teach and improve the standards of transparency and credibility in research reports made by students [1]. It aims to embed students in transparent and open practices from the beginning of their training [1].

Here's how it can be used:

*   Supervisors and instructors can require students to create a Transparency Report along with any empirical research assignment [1].
*   Instructors can require completion of the checklist, and make the checklist app available to students [1]. You can use either the full checklist: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1NxJG5ccRAhvLKngosRVjT8IO2OZ0UDZMN86FW5qGf0Q/edit?usp=sharing](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1NxJG5ccRAhvLKngosRVjT8IO2OZ0UDZMN86FW5qGf0Q/edit?usp=sharing) or the Short Checklist: [http://www.shinyapps.org/apps/ShortTransparencyChecklist/](http://www.shinyapps.org/apps/ShortTransparencyChecklist/) [1].
*   The checklist was developed through consensus among 45 journal editors and 18 open-science advocates [1].

You can find more information about the checklist in this paper: [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-019-0772-6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-019-0772-6) [1].

question: What is a Registered Report and how does it change the peer review process in scientific publishing?
answer:
A Registered Report is a publication format where the methods are peer-reviewed and accepted *before* data are collected [1]. This is especially valuable for replications because the acceptance decision is no longer based on the results, which reduces bias towards smaller, null, or inconclusive findings that replications often produce [1].

Specifically, with Registered Reports, a special review platform called Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI-RR) is used, where a community reviews pre-prints [1]. Once accepted by PCI-RR, authors can publish their paper in participating journals (PCI friendly journals) without another editorial round [1].

You can find a list of journals offering Registered Reports [available online](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0) [1]. You can also find more information about Registered Reports at [https://rr.peercommunityin.org](https://rr.peercommunityin.org) [1].

question: What is FORRT?
answer:
FORRT is a **F**ramework for **O**pen and **R**eproducible **R**esearch **T**raining advancing research transparency, reproducibility, rigor, and ethics through pedagogical reform and meta-scientific research [1][2]. It provides a pedagogical infrastructure & didactic resources designed to recognize and support the teaching and mentoring of open and reproducible science [1][2]. 

FORRT strives to raise awareness of the pedagogical implications of open and reproducible science and advocates for the opening and formal recognition of teaching and mentoring materials [1][2]. Its goals include building a pathway for the adoption of open and reproducible science tenets in education, fostering a conversation about the ethics and social impact of open scholarship, advocating for recognition of teaching and mentoring, and fostering social justice through the democratization of scientific-educational resources [3].

You can learn more [About FORRT](https://forrt.org/#3-what-is-forrt) or [Get involved](https://forrt.org/about/get-involved/). You can also view the [FORRT Booklet](https://forrt.org/booklet/) [2].

question: How can I get involved with FORRT?
answer:
You can get involved with FORRT in several ways [1][3]. The majority of FORRT’s operations are done via their [Slack channel](https://join.slack.com/t/forrt/shared_invite/zt-alobr3z7-NOR0mTBfD1vKXn9qlOKqaQ) [1].

This document is organized into three parts: general information, current initiatives, and the FORRT organization [1].

There are also several ongoing projects where collaborators are welcome, such as FLoRA ([https://forrt.org/replication-hub/flora/](https://forrt.org/replication-hub/flora/)), Lighthouse, Best-Practice Guidelines for Psychology ([https://forrt.org/best-practices-psychology/](https://forrt.org/best-practices-psychology/)), Re-SearchTerms ([https://forrt.org/apps/re-searchterms.html](https://forrt.org/apps/re-searchterms.html)), Mapping Open Science Communities ([https://forrt.org/mapping_os/](https://forrt.org/mapping_os/)), OS Games Portal ([https://forrt.org/open-research-games-portal/](https://forrt.org/open-research-games-portal/)), and more [1]. You can find contact information for each project on the “Ongoing Projects” page.

Additionally, you can join specific teams like Team Credit ([https://forrt.slack.com/archives/C082GR7P04X](https://forrt.slack.com/archives/C082GR7P04X)), Team Outreach ([https://forrt.slack.com/archives/C0184989HHC](https://forrt.slack.com/archives/C0184989HHC)), or Team Website ([https://forrt.slack.com/archives/C080N39QRJ9](https://forrt.slack.com/archives/C080N39QRJ9)) via Slack [1][3]. Finally, you can find more information and links on the [Get Involved page](https://forrt.org/about/get-involved/) [3][4].

question: Who can I talk to confidentially about a code of conduct problem?
answer:
You can talk to either the Confidential Advisor or the Ombuds confidentially about a code of conduct problem [2]. 

The Confidential Advisor is Ruth Van der Hallen, PhD, and can be reached at [confidential-advisor@forrt.org](mailto:confidential-advisor@forrt.org) [2]. They provide support and guidance regarding inappropriate behaviour, interpersonal conflicts, or concerns related to integrity [2].

The Ombuds is Thomas Rhys Evans, and can be reached at [ombuds@forrt.org](mailto:ombuds@forrt.org) [2]. They address concerns about FORRT policies, practices, or processes [2].

Both roles treat conversations with care and confidentiality, and will not share information without consent unless there is a serious risk of harm [2]. You can also report a suspected code of conduct violation through this anonymous form: [Access link here.](https://forms.gle/nQ51x1c8a8nnfQ7a9) [1]. 

Additionally, you can reach out to the Confidential Advisor or Ombuds to discuss a concern before filing a report [1].

question: What is the Nowhere Lab?
answer:
Nowhere Lab is a remote, global lab for everyone [1]. It’s an online community for people who would like the lab meeting experience but don’t currently have one [1]. Members include people from all populated continents and career stages, such as undergraduate students, Ph.D. students, and those working outside of academia [1]. 

Nowhere Lab partnered with FORRT to promote social justice and enable equality of access to open scholarship training [1]. Members benefit from weekly meetings and can ask questions about open scholarship practices [1]. It was started in 2020 when the founder missed having a lab community after moving to alt-ac roles [3]. 

You can join by emailing [priyasilverstein@gmail.com](mailto:priyasilverstein@gmail.com) [1][3]. You can also join their [Slack channel](https://forrt.slack.com/archives/C0B0FKG3GH2) [2][3] and read more on their website [https://forrt.org/nowherelab/](https://forrt.org/nowherelab/) [3]. They also have a [PhD Survival Guide](https://forrt.org/nowherelab/phd-survival-guide/) [3].

Weekly meetings are held Tuesdays at 9am (UK) and Thursdays at 4pm (UK), lasting approximately 1 hour [3].

question: What is the Academic Wheel of Privilege?
answer:
The Academic Wheel of Privilege (AWoP) is an equity-based tool for authorship order [1]. It aims to address imbalances in research impact and professional advancement by considering justice and equity, and to reduce credit disparities for marginalized researchers [1]. 

The AWoP includes a web app, manuscript, and supplementary files [1][2]. The app generates customized weighted indicators of privilege across socio-economic and cultural identity categories [1][2]. Supplemental materials include reflection questions, a case study on first-generation academics, illustrated examples of privilege/disadvantage, a detailed bibliography, and a syllabus for learning on equity, justice, and accessibility [1].

The AWoP is being used by the [UK Research Integrity Office (UKRIO)](https://ukrio.org/ukrio-resources/equality-diversity-and-inclusion/academic-wheel-of-privilege/) [1].

You can access the [AWoP Web App](https://forrt.org/awop_app/) [1][2] and find the manuscript at [https://doi.org/10.31222/osf.io/af4nk_v2](https://doi.org/10.31222/osf.io/af4nk_v2) [1].  You can also find supplementary files on the [OSF page](https://osf.io/pfxqb/overview) [1].

For more information, you can contact the team at [awop@forrt.org](mailto:awop@forrt.org) [1].

question: What does FORRT offer on neurodiversity?
answer:
FORRT has a dedicated Team Neurodiversity that discusses how open scholarship can support the neurodiversity movement and enhance inclusivity [2]. The team believes that neurodiversity and open scholarship share fundamental principles of social justice, diversity, equity, and inclusion [2]. 

They aim to highlight barriers faced by neurodivergent academics and promote acceptance, inclusion, and support [2]. They are developing resources about neurodiversity in academia, and currently have a piece in the Association for Psychological Science’s Observer magazine [2]. 

FORRT’s Neurodiversity team advocates for recognizing neurodivergent experiences as fundamental to the human experience, rather than pathologizing them [2]. They emphasize the importance of listening to disabled individuals and providing accommodations [2].

You can learn more about their work and join the team via [Slack](https://forrt.slack.com/archives/C0B0FKG3GH2) and find their position statement here: [https://osf.io/preprints/metaarxiv/k7a9p/](https://osf.io/preprints/metaarxiv/k7a9p/) [2]. They also mention a resource on Universal Design for Learning [2]. 

The team references Grinker, 2010, stating “Their strengths and deficits do not deny them humanity but, rather, shape their humanity” [2].

question: What is the JUST-OS chatbot?

It aims to help researchers navigate Open Science resources more easily by providing user-friendly, tailored, and efficient guidance [1][2].

JUST-OS writes its answers with OpenScholar (Llama-3.1_OpenScholar-8B) [1]. If you use or write about JUST-OS, you should cite Asai et al. (2026): Asai, A., He, J., Shao, R., et al. (2026). Synthesizing scientific literature with retrieval-augmented language models. Nature, 650(8103), 857–863. [<https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-10072-4>] [1].

question: Is there a Chinese version of the FORRT glossary?
answer:
Yes, FORRT’s Glossary of Open Scholarship terms is now available in Chinese [1]. This lowers the barrier to understanding and participating in open-science discussions for Chinese-speaking researchers and students [1]. You can [Explore the glossary](https://forrt.org/glossary/chinese/) [1].

You can also find the Chinese glossary listed alongside other language versions here: [https://forrt.org/glossary/](https://forrt.org/glossary/) [2]. 

The Chinese-language glossary was published on 2026-05-31 [1], so that event took place in the past.

question: What awards has FORRT received?
answer:
FORRT has received several awards and recognitions [1]. 

In 2026, FORRT received **The Leo Waaijers Open Science Award** from the NWO UKB, celebrating its work [1][2].

question: What is new at FORRT?
answer:
FORRT has been awarded the Leo Waaijers Open Science Award 2026 [1]. FORRT was also well represented at the Big Team Science Conference 2026 [1]. Recordings of 32 talks from the FORRT AI in Metascience Online Conference (28–30 September 2026) are now available on the FORRT YouTube channel [1]. 

FORRT has added Peer Community In (PCI) and the Peer Community Journal to its network of partners [1]. The Glossary of Open Scholarship is now available in Chinese [1]. 

FORRT welcomes Nowhere Lab into its community, and you can join their channel on Slack [1]. The JUST-OS chatbot is now live on the website [1].

The Get Involved page has been updated [1].

FORRT launched the FORWARD initiative aligned with UNESCO’s International Decade of Sciences for Sustainable Development [4]. They are also preparing for the FORRT AI in Metascience Online Conference (28–30 September 2026) and are accepting submissions until 31 July 2026 [3]. The Open Research Games Portal is now available [3]. The inaugural editorial of Replication Research (R2) is now online [3]. Love Replications Week took place from March 2–6 [4]. The Making Replications Count Hackathon took place from May 4–6 [4].

Feedback welcome: [lukas.roeseler@uni-muenster.de](mailto:lukas.roeseler@uni-muenster.de) or [GitHub](https://github.com/forrtproject/replication-handbook/issues). Tip **Key takeaways** Reproductions and replications require clarifying whether the aim is to verify a method or test a broader theory, as this determines the choice between close and conceptual approaches. question: What is a registered report?
answer:
A Registered Report is a format where the methods are peer-reviewed and accepted for publication before data are collected [1]. This format is especially valuable for replications because the acceptance decision no longer depends on the nature of the results, reducing bias against smaller, null, or inconclusive findings [1]. A list of journals offering Registered Reports is [available online](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0) [1]. 

There is also a special review platform for Registered Reports called Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI-RR) [<https://rr.peercommunityin.org>] [1], where a community reviews pre-prints, and accepted papers can be published in participating journals without further editorial review [1].

question: Wie kann ich bei FORRT mitmachen?
answer:

question: ¿Qué es FORRT?
answer:
FORRT is a **F**ramework for **O**pen and **R**eproducible **R**esearch **T**raining advancing research transparency, reproducibility, rigor, and ethics through pedagogical reform and meta-scientific research [1][2]. It provides a pedagogical infrastructure & didactic resources designed to recognize and support the teaching and mentoring of open and reproducible science [1][2]. 

FORRT strives to raise awareness of the pedagogical implications of open and reproducible science and advocates for the opening and formal recognition of teaching and mentoring materials [2]. It aims to familiarize higher-ED students with the intricacies of the process of science [2].

FORRT supports educators through a three-pronged approach: providing a framework to teach and mentor open and reproducible science, equipping educators with high quality pedagogical tools, and modifying the academic incentive structure regarding teaching and mentoring [2].

You can learn more [About FORRT](https://forrt.org/#3-what-is-forrt) or [Get involved](https://forrt.org/about/get-involved/) [1]. You can also view the [FORRT Booklet](https://forrt.org/booklet/) [2].

question: What is Re-SearchTerms?
answer:
Re-SearchTerms is an open, interactive app for exploring how research terms are defined across sources and contexts, and for identifying terminological variabilities [3]. Its core aims are to build an open, pedagogical infrastructure that supports users to make more deliberate and transparent use of research terminology, working in alignment with the development of the FORRT glossary [3]. 

You can [check out the app](https://msleungyi.shinyapps.io/Re-SearchTerms_v2/) and a [newly accepted paper](https://osf.io/preprints/osf/qsp7x_v3) about it in Meta-Psychology [3]. The project is currently recruiting contributors to expand the dataset and enrich app features [3]. You can message the Project Lead, Anna Yi Leung, on Slack [3].

The platform allows you to compare definitions, examine relationships between terms and definitions, and analyse patterns in the language used to describe core concepts in research [1]. It was originally developed as part of a doctoral dissertation examining conceptual variability and terminological ambiguity [1].

question: How can I contribute definitions of research terms in German or Chinese?
answer:
You can contribute definitions of research terms in English, German, or Chinese by joining as a contributor [1]. This involves submitting source-based definitions, translating definitions from existing sources, or annotating and verifying existing entries [1]. All contributors are publicly recognised [1].

You can also contribute by adding definitions to the working documents linked here: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1IpkueFstVauvKrvgd-0OddAeAr2YGReY2IiSJILmY2I](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1IpkueFstVauvKrvgd-0OddAeAr2YGReY2IiSJILmY2I) and [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OV1WKyLMmCvcrHaO9iVCdxOGVxoEza4yjvdT6Q5ZBKE](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OV1WKyLMmCvcrHaO9iVCdxOGVxoEza4yjvdT6Q5ZBKE) [2].
